question: When machines arrived to do part of the translator's and interpreter's job (1954 prediction, 1966 verdict, today), did the humans disappear, or did the work change, and which part stays with people and for how long?

issues.note: Cut from the split-screen 1966 vs today comparison to a wide, static shot of an empty-feeling office. Narration 'The change shows up in the...' starts over a picture that shows nothing of the change, so it feels abrupt.
Cut from the 1966 office to the library street. The narration moves to a new idea ('the committee also found a machine') over a picture of the lamplighter, so the picture and narration do not match.
The Nuremberg and today split-screen is a fast, busy cut. The narration then jumps to 'the next ten years?' over a static video-call room, and the Nuremberg callback comes with no setup.

The narration 'Cannot yet. Here is the comparison we can make' sits over a 1966 typed-page close-up, though the frame cuts away from the editor screen mid-sentence. The topic shifts from BLS data to a theme comparison with no bridge.

The cut moves from a Red Cross archive photo to the Nuremberg booths. The narration jump is understandable but the cut is hard, with no bridging picture. The caption 'a few years later: a trial' is the only link.
The 1966 office scene (R07.2-R07.4) and later office frames repeat the same static wide shot for several samples, with little new to see.
R12.7-R13.2 hold the same office and monitor view for about 24 s, with only captions changing, around the data-heavy stretch on jobs and statistics.
R15.4-R15.8 are all close-ups of the same translation editor screen, with no new picture while the narration repeats the 'cannot yet' idea.
